summary: The note traces Halloween from the ancient Celtic festival of Samhain through its Christianization and its later lighthearted, commercial and global forms. It covers Celtic beliefs about the thinning boundary between living and dead, the creation of All Saints' Day, the origin of jack-o'-lanterns and trick-or-treating, and parallels with festivals like Dia de los Muertos. It cites several researchers whose work supports each stage of this evolution.
one_line: Halloween evolved from the Celtic festival of Samhain through Christian influence into a lighthearted global celebration with echoes of ancient spirit-appeasing customs.
key_facts: Samhain (pronounced 'sow-in') was celebrated by the Celts in pre-Christian Ireland, Scotland, and the Isle of Man, marking the end of the harvest and the start of the 'darker half' of the year.
The Celts celebrated Samhain on November 1st and believed the boundary between the living and the dead blurred, letting spirits and fairies, or 'Aos Sí,' roam the earth.
Dr. Fiona Byrne's team, on September 5, 2023, uncovered artifacts near the Hill of Tara in Ireland indicating the lighting of sacred bonfires believed to have protective and cleansing power.
Celtic communal bonfires were used to offer sacrifices of crops and animals for the coming winter.
Folklore specialist Aiden O'Neill (published October 12, 2023) described Celtic divination and offerings, such as plates of food set out and doors and windows left open for spirits.
Pope Gregory III designated November 1st as All Saints' Day (All Hallows' Day) in the eighth century, so the evening before became All Hallows' Eve and later Halloween.
Historian Madeleine Kearns reportedly unearthed manuscripts dated to 2024 showing deliberate Church efforts to supplant pagan practices with Christian traditions.

Carving jack-o'-lanterns stems from an Irish folk tale about Stingy Jack, who roamed the night with a hollowed-out turnip; Irish immigrants in North America adopted the easier-to-carve native pumpkin.
Amelia Brown's study, published October 20, 2023, explored how Halloween shifted from fear and appeasement to revelry and play.
Trick-or-treat evolved from 'guising' in Scotland and Ireland, where people in costumes performed in exchange for food or coins.
Professor James Collier's commentary (September 15, 2023) noted that trick-or-treating resembles the ancient practice of placating wandering spirits with gifts.
Claudia Schmidt's comparative study (October 8, 2023) highlighted resemblances between Halloween and festivals such as Mexico's Dia de los Muertos and China's Hungry Ghost Festival.
